title: 16. The execution
paragraphs: The sun was already descending over Bald Mountain, and this mountain was cordoned off by a double cordon.

The cavalry ala that had cut across the procurator’s path around noon came out at a trot to the Hebron Gate of the city. The way had already been prepared for it. The infantrymen of the Cappadocian cohort had pressed back to the sides the crowds of people, mules and camels, and the ala, trotting and raising white columns of dust to the sky, came out at the crossroads where two roads met: the southern one, leading to Bethlehem, and the northwestern one, to Jaffa. The ala raced along the northwestern road. The same Cappadocians were scattered along the edges of the road, and they had driven off it in good time all the caravans hurrying to the feast in Yershalaim. Crowds of pilgrims stood behind the Cappadocians, having left their temporary striped tents pitched right on the grass. After going about a kilometer, the ala overtook the second cohort of the Lightning Legion and, covering another kilometer, was the first to reach the foot of Bald Mountain. Here it dismounted. The commander split the ala into troops, and they cordoned off the whole foot of the low hill, leaving free only one way up it, from the Jaffa road.
After a while the second cohort came to the hill behind the ala, climbed one tier higher, and girdled the mountain like a crown.

At last the century under the command of Mark Ratslayer arrived. It came stretched out in two lines along the edges of the road, and between these lines, under escort of the secret guard, rode in a cart the three condemned men, with white boards around their necks, on each of which was written “Robber and rebel” in two languages, Aramaic and Greek.

Behind the cart of the condemned moved others, loaded with freshly hewn posts with crossbeams, ropes, shovels, buckets and axes. On these carts rode six executioners. Behind them on horseback rode the centurion Mark, the head of the Yershalaim temple guard, and that same man in the hood with whom Pilate had held a brief conference in the darkened room in the palace.

The procession was closed by a line of soldiers, and behind it walked some two thousand curious people who had not been frightened off by the hellish heat and wished to be present at the interesting spectacle.

These curious people from the city had now been joined by curious pilgrims, who were let through without hindrance to the tail of the procession. To the thin cries of the heralds who accompanied the column and called out what Pilate had called out around noon, it wound its way up onto Bald Mountain.

The ala let everyone through to the second tier, but the second century let through to the top only those who had to do with the execution, and then, maneuvering quickly, it dispersed the crowd around the whole hill, so that it found itself between the infantry cordon above and the cavalry one below. Now it could watch the execution through the loose line of infantrymen.

And so, more than three hours had passed since the procession had climbed the mountain, and the sun was already descending over Bald Mountain, but the heat was still unbearable, and the soldiers in both cordons suffered from it, languished with boredom, and in their hearts cursed the three robbers, sincerely wishing them the swiftest death.

The little commander of the ala, his forehead soaked and his white shirt dark with sweat on the back, who was stationed at the bottom of the hill by the open way up, kept going over to the leather bucket of the first troop, scooping water out of it in handfuls, drinking, and wetting his turban. Having got some relief from this, he would walk away and again begin pacing back and forth along the dusty road leading to the top. His long sword knocked against his laced leather boot. The commander wished to show his cavalrymen an example of endurance, but, taking pity on the soldiers, he allowed them to make pyramids of the lances stuck into the ground and throw their white cloaks over them. Under these shelters the Syrians hid from the merciless sun. The buckets emptied quickly, and cavalrymen from the different troops took turns going for water to the gully below the mountain, where, in the thin shade of scrawny mulberry trees, a muddy stream was living out its last days in this devilish heat. There too, catching the unsteady shade, stood the bored grooms, holding the horses, which had grown quiet.

The soldiers’ weariness and their curses against the robbers were understandable. The procurator’s fears about disorders that might occur during the execution in the city of Yershalaim, which he hated, had, fortunately, not been borne out. And when the fourth hour of the execution began to run, there remained between the two lines, the infantry above and the cavalry at the foot, contrary to all expectations, not a single person. The sun had burned up the crowd and driven it back to Yershalaim. Beyond the line of the two Roman centuries there were only two dogs, belonging to no one knew whom and come onto the hill for no one knew what reason. But the heat had overcome them too, and they lay down with their tongues hanging out, breathing heavily and paying no attention at all to the green-backed lizards, the only creatures not afraid of the sun, darting between the scorching stones and some sort of plants with large thorns that crept along the ground.

No one had made an attempt to rescue the condemned men, either in Yershalaim itself, flooded with troops, or here on the cordoned hill, and the crowd had gone back to the city, because there was indeed absolutely nothing interesting in this execution, while there in the city preparations were already under way for the great feast of Passover, which would begin that evening.

The Roman infantry on the second tier suffered even more than the cavalrymen. The only thing the centurion Ratslayer allowed the soldiers was to take off their helmets and cover their heads with white bands soaked in water, but he kept the soldiers standing, spears in hand. He himself, in the same kind of band, though not soaked but dry, strolled about not far from the group of executioners, not having removed even the silver lion masks sewn onto his shirt, nor his greaves, sword and knife. The sun beat straight down on the centurion without doing him any harm, and it was impossible to look at the lion masks: the blinding glitter stung the eyes of silver that seemed to be boiling in the sun.

Ratslayer’s mutilated face showed neither fatigue nor displeasure, and it seemed that the giant centurion was capable of walking like this all day, all night and another day—in short, as long as might be needed. Of walking just the same, his hands on his heavy belt with its copper plaques, just as sternly glancing now at the posts with the men being executed, now at the soldiers in the line, just as indifferently kicking aside with the toe of his shaggy boot the human bones bleached by time or the small flints that came under his feet.
That man in the hood had settled himself not far from the posts on a three-legged stool and sat in good-humored immobility, though now and then, out of boredom, he poked at the sand with a twig.

What was said about there being not a single person beyond the line of legionaries is not quite true. There was one person, it is just that not everyone could see him. He had settled himself not on the side where the way up the mountain was open, from which it was most convenient to watch the execution, but on the northern side, where the hill was not gently sloping and easy of access but uneven, where there were both hollows and crevices, there, where, clinging in a cleft to the waterless earth cursed by heaven, a sickly little fig tree was trying to live.

It was precisely under it, though it gave no shade whatsoever, that this sole spectator, and not participant, of the execution had established himself, and he had been sitting on a stone from the very beginning, that is, for nearly four hours now. Yes, to watch the execution he had chosen not the best but the worst position. Yet even from there the posts could be seen, and beyond the line the two glittering spots on the centurion’s chest could be seen too, and for a man who clearly wished to remain little noticed and disturbed by no one, this was evidently quite enough.

But about four hours earlier, at the beginning of the execution, this man had behaved quite differently and could very well have been noticed, which was probably why he had now changed his behavior and withdrawn on his own.

Back then, the moment the procession had passed through the line to the very top, he appeared for the first time, and moreover as a man who was clearly late. He was breathing heavily and was not walking but running up the hill, pushing his way along, and when he saw that the line had closed before him, as before everyone else, he made a naive attempt, pretending not to understand the irritated shouts, to break through between the soldiers to the very place of execution, where the condemned were already being taken down from the cart. For this he received a heavy blow in the chest from the blunt end of a spear and sprang back from the soldiers with a cry, not of pain but of despair. He gave the legionary who had struck him a dull look, utterly indifferent to everything, like a man insensible to physical pain.

Coughing and gasping for breath, holding his chest, he ran around the hill, trying to find on the northern side some gap in the line through which he could slip. But it was already too late. The ring had closed. And the man, his face distorted with grief, was forced to give up his attempts to break through to the carts, from which the posts had already been unloaded. These attempts would have led to nothing except his being seized, and to be detained on this day was in no way part of his plans.
And so he had gone off to the side, to the cleft, where it was quieter and no one bothered him.

Now, sitting on the stone, this black-bearded man, his eyes festering from the sun and from lack of sleep, was in anguish. Now he sighed, opening his tallif, worn out in his wanderings, which had turned from blue to a dirty gray, and bared his chest, bruised by the spear, down which dirty sweat was running; now, in unbearable torment, he raised his eyes to the sky, following the three vultures that had long been floating high above in great circles in anticipation of an imminent feast; now he fixed a hopeless gaze on the yellow earth and saw on it a half-crumbled dog’s skull and lizards running around it.
The man’s torments were so great that at times he began talking to himself.
“Oh, I am a fool!” he muttered, rocking on the stone in anguish of soul and scratching his swarthy chest with his nails. “A fool, a senseless woman, a coward! Carrion is what I am, not a man!”

He would fall silent, hang his head, then, having drunk some warm water from a wooden flask, revive again and clutch now at the knife hidden under the tallif on his chest, now at a piece of parchment lying before him on the stone next to a stick and a little bottle of ink.
On this parchment some notes had already been jotted down:
“The minutes are running, and I, Levi Matvei, am on Bald Mountain, and still there is no death!”
Further on:
“The sun is sinking, and there is no death.”
Now Levi Matvei hopelessly wrote with the sharpened stick:
“God! Why are you angry with him? Send him death.”
Having written this, he gave a tearless sob and again wounded his chest with his nails.

The cause of Levi’s despair lay in the terrible misfortune that had befallen Yeshua and himself, and, besides that, in the grave mistake which he, Levi, had in his own opinion made. The day before yesterday, in the daytime, Yeshua and Levi had been in Bethany near Yershalaim, where they were staying with a market gardener who had been greatly taken with Yeshua’s preaching. Both guests had worked all morning in the garden, helping their host, and toward evening they meant to walk to Yershalaim in the cool. But Yeshua for some reason grew hurried, said he had urgent business in the city, and left alone around noon. This was precisely where Levi Matvei’s first mistake lay. Why, why had he let him go alone!

In the evening Matvei was not able to go to Yershalaim. Some unexpected and terrible ailment struck him. He began to shake, his body filled with fire, his teeth began to chatter, and every minute he asked for something to drink. He could not go anywhere. He collapsed onto a horse blanket in the gardener’s shed and lay on it until the dawn of Friday, when the illness let go of Levi just as unexpectedly as it had attacked him. Though he was still weak and his legs trembled, he, tormented by some foreboding of disaster, took leave of his host and set off for Yershalaim. There he learned that his foreboding had not deceived him. Disaster had struck. Levi was in the crowd and heard the procurator announce the sentence.

When the condemned men were driven to the mountain, Levi Matvei ran alongside the line in the crowd of the curious, trying by some means to let Yeshua know, without being noticed, at least this much: that he, Levi, was here, with him, that he had not abandoned him on his last journey, and that he was praying for death to overtake Yeshua as quickly as possible. But Yeshua, looking into the distance, toward where he was being taken, did not, of course, see Levi.

And then, when the procession had gone about half a verst along the road, Matvei, who was being jostled in the crowd right by the line, was struck by a simple and brilliant thought, and at once, in his hot-headedness, he showered himself with curses for not having thought of it earlier. The soldiers were not marching in a tight line. There were gaps between them. With great agility and very precise calculation one could, bending low, slip between two legionaries, get through to the cart and leap onto it. Then Yeshua would be saved from torment.
One instant would be enough to stab Yeshua in the back with a knife, crying out to him: “Yeshua! I am saving you and going with you! I, Matvei, your faithful and only disciple!”

And if God blessed him with one more free instant, there might be time to stab himself too, escaping death on a post. However, this last point interested Levi, the former tax collector, very little. It made no difference to him how he perished. He wanted one thing: that Yeshua, who had never in his life done anyone the slightest harm, should escape torture.
The plan was very good, but the point was that Levi had no knife with him. Nor did he have a single coin of money.

Furious with himself, Levi got out of the crowd and ran back to the city. In his burning head leaped only one feverish thought: how, right now, by any means whatever, to get hold of a knife in the city and manage to catch up with the procession.

He ran as far as the city gate, weaving through the crush of caravans being sucked into the city, and saw on his left hand the open door of a little shop where bread was sold. Breathing heavily after running along the scorching road, Levi mastered himself, walked into the shop very sedately, greeted the woman who kept it, standing behind the counter, asked her to take down from the shelf the top loaf, which for some reason he liked better than the others, and, when she turned round, silently and quickly took from the counter the very thing that could not have been better—a long bread knife, sharpened like a razor—and at once dashed out of the shop.

A few minutes later he was again on the Jaffa road. But the procession could no longer be seen. He ran. At times he had to drop right down into the dust and lie motionless to get his breath back. And so he lay, astonishing the people riding on mules and walking on foot to Yershalaim. He lay listening to his heart pounding not only in his chest but in his head and in his ears. Having got his breath back a little, he would leap up and run on, but more and more slowly. When at last he caught sight of the long procession raising dust in the distance, it was already at the foot of the hill.
“O God...” Levi groaned, understanding that he was going to be late. And he was late.

When the fourth hour of the execution had run out, Levi’s torments reached their highest pitch, and he fell into a rage. Rising from the stone, he flung to the ground the knife, stolen in vain, as he now thought, crushed the flask with his foot, depriving himself of water, threw the kefi off his head, seized his thin hair, and began to curse himself.
He cursed himself, shouting out senseless words, growled and spat, reviled his father and mother for bringing a fool into the world.

Seeing that his oaths and abuse had no effect and that nothing changed in the blazing sun because of them, he clenched his dry fists, shut his eyes tight, raised them to the sky, to the sun, which was creeping lower and lower, lengthening the shadows and going away to fall into the Mediterranean Sea, and demanded of God an immediate miracle. He demanded that God send Yeshua death at once.

Opening his eyes, he satisfied himself that on the hill everything was unchanged, except that the spots blazing on the centurion’s chest had gone out. The sun was sending its rays into the backs of the men being executed, who were turned with their faces toward Yershalaim. Then Levi shouted:
“I curse you, God!”
In a hoarse voice he shouted that he had become convinced of God’s injustice and did not intend to believe in him any longer.
“You are deaf!” Levi growled. “If you were not deaf, you would have heard me and killed him on the spot!”

Squeezing his eyes shut, Levi waited for the fire that would fall on him from the sky and strike him down. This did not happen, and, without unclenching his eyelids, Levi went on shouting caustic and insulting speeches at the sky. He shouted about his complete disillusionment and about there being other gods and religions. Yes, another god would not have allowed it, would never have allowed a man like Yeshua to be burned by the sun on a post.

“I was wrong!” shouted Levi, by now quite hoarse. “You are a god of evil! Or have your eyes been completely covered by the smoke from the censers of the temple, and have your ears ceased to hear anything but the trumpet blasts of the priests? You are not an almighty God. You are a black god. I curse you, god of robbers, their protector and their soul!”

At this something blew into the former tax collector’s face and something rustled under his feet. It blew again, and then, opening his eyes, Levi saw that everything in the world, whether under the influence of his curses or by virtue of some other causes, had changed. The sun had vanished before reaching the sea in which it drowned every evening. Having swallowed it, a storm cloud was rising across the sky from the west, menacingly and inexorably. Its edges were already boiling with white foam, its black smoky belly glinted yellow. The cloud was growling, and from time to time fiery threads fell out of it. Along the Jaffa road, along the meager Gihon valley, over the pilgrims’ tents, driven by the suddenly risen wind, columns of dust were flying.

Levi fell silent, trying to work out whether the storm that was about to cover Yershalaim would bring any change in the fate of the unfortunate Yeshua. And straight away, looking at the threads of fire slicing the cloud apart, he began to beg that the lightning might strike Yeshua’s post. Looking in repentance at the clear sky, which the cloud had not yet devoured and where the vultures were banking on the wing to get away from the storm, Levi thought that he had been insanely hasty with his curses: now God would not listen to him.

Turning his gaze to the foot of the hill, Levi fixed his eyes on the place where the cavalry regiment stood, spread out, and saw that significant changes had taken place there. From the height Levi managed to make out clearly how the soldiers were bustling about, pulling the lances out of the ground, how they were throwing their cloaks on, how the grooms were running toward the road at a jog, leading black horses by the bridle. The regiment was moving off, that was clear. Levi, shielding himself with his hand from the dust beating into his face and spitting, tried to work out what this could mean, that the cavalry was getting ready to leave? He shifted his gaze higher and made out a small figure in a crimson military chlamys climbing toward the place of execution. And at this the former tax collector’s heart went cold with the foreboding of a joyful end.

The man climbing the mountain in the fifth hour of the robbers’ sufferings was the commander of the cohort, who had galloped from Yershalaim accompanied by an orderly. At a wave from Ratslayer the line of soldiers opened, and the centurion saluted the tribune. The tribune, taking Ratslayer aside, whispered something to him. The centurion saluted a second time and moved toward the group of executioners who were sitting on stones at the foot of the posts. The tribune, for his part, directed his steps toward the one sitting on the three-legged stool, and the seated man politely rose to meet the tribune. The tribune said something to him too, in a low voice, and the two of them walked toward the posts. They were joined by the head of the temple guard as well.

Ratslayer, glancing with disgust at the dirty rags lying on the ground by the posts, rags that had recently been the criminals’ clothes, which the executioners had refused, called two of them over and ordered:
“Follow me!”

From the nearest post came a hoarse, senseless little song. Gestas, who hung on it, had gone mad from the flies and the sun by the end of the third hour of the execution and was now quietly singing something about grapes, but still, now and then, he shook his head, covered with a turban, and then the flies rose sluggishly from his face and came back onto it again.

Dismas, on the second post, suffered more than the other two, because oblivion did not overcome him, and he shook his head often and rhythmically, now to the right, now to the left, so as to strike his shoulder with his ear.

Yeshua was more fortunate than the other two. In the very first hour fainting fits began to strike him, and then he sank into oblivion, his head hanging in its unwound turban. The flies and horseflies had therefore covered him completely, so that his face disappeared under a black, stirring mask. In his groin, and on his belly, and under his arms sat fat horseflies, sucking at the yellow naked body.

Obeying the gestures of the man in the hood, one of the executioners took a spear, while another brought a bucket and a sponge to the post. The first executioner raised the spear and tapped with it first on one and then on the other of Yeshua’s arms, stretched out and tied with ropes to the crossbeam of the post. The body with its protruding ribs shuddered. The executioner drew the tip of the spear across the belly. Then Yeshua raised his head, and the flies lifted off with a buzz, and the face of the hanged man was revealed, swollen from bites, with puffed-up eyes, an unrecognizable face.
Unsticking his eyelids, Ha-Notsri looked down. His eyes, usually clear, were now somewhat clouded.
“Ha-Notsri!” said the executioner.
Ha-Notsri moved his swollen lips and responded in a hoarse robber’s voice:
“What do you want? Why have you come up to me?”

“Drink!” said the executioner, and the sponge soaked in water on the end of the spear rose to Yeshua’s lips. Joy flashed in his eyes; he pressed his mouth to the sponge and began greedily drinking in the moisture. From the neighboring post came the voice of Dismas:
“Injustice! I’m as much a robber as he is!”

Dismas strained, but could not move; his arms were held to the crossbeam in three places by loops of rope. He drew in his belly, dug his nails into the ends of the crossbeam, kept his head turned toward Yeshua’s post, and malice blazed in Dismas’s eyes.
A cloud of dust covered the place of execution, and it grew much darker. When the dust had blown away, the centurion shouted:
“Silence on the second post!”
Dismas fell silent. Yeshua tore himself away from the sponge and, trying to make his voice sound gentle and persuasive, and not succeeding, hoarsely asked the executioner:
“Give him a drink.”

It was growing darker and darker. The cloud had already flooded half the sky, pressing on toward Yershalaim; white boiling clouds raced ahead of the storm cloud, which was saturated with black moisture and fire. There was a flash and a crash right over the hill. The executioner took the sponge off the spear.
“Praise the magnanimous hegemon!” he whispered solemnly, and gently pierced Yeshua in the heart. Yeshua shuddered and whispered:
“Hegemon...”
Blood ran down his belly, his lower jaw twitched convulsively, and his head dropped.
At the second thunderclap the executioner was already giving Dismas a drink, and with the same words:
“Praise the hegemon!”—he killed him too.

Gestas, bereft of reason, gave a frightened cry as soon as the executioner was beside him, but when the sponge touched his lips, he growled something and sank his teeth into it. A few seconds later his body too sagged as far as the ropes allowed.

The man in the hood followed in the footsteps of the executioner and the centurion, and behind him came the head of the temple guard. Stopping at the first post, the man in the hood examined the bloodied Yeshua attentively, touched a foot with his white hand, and said to his companions:
“Dead.”
The same thing was repeated at the two other posts.

After this the tribune made a sign to the centurion and, turning, began to leave the top together with the head of the temple guard and the man in the hood. Half-darkness had fallen, and lightning furrowed the black sky. Suddenly fire spurted from it, and the centurion’s shout, “Break the cordon!” was drowned in the thunder. The happy soldiers rushed down the hill, putting on their helmets.
Darkness covered Yershalaim.

The downpour burst suddenly and caught the centuries halfway down the hill. The water came crashing down so terribly that, as the soldiers ran downhill, raging torrents were already flying after them. The soldiers slipped and fell in the sodden clay, hurrying to the level road along which—now barely visible through the curtain of water—the cavalry, soaked to the skin, was leaving for Yershalaim. A few minutes later, in the smoky brew of storm, water and fire, only one man remained on the hill.

Brandishing the knife he had not stolen in vain after all, slipping from the slippery ledges, clutching at whatever came to hand, sometimes crawling on his knees, he struggled toward the posts. Now he vanished in total murk, now he was suddenly lit up by a quivering light.

Reaching the posts, by now ankle-deep in water, he tore off his tallif, grown heavy and soaked through with water, was left in his shirt alone, and fell at Yeshua’s feet. He cut the ropes on his shins, climbed onto the lower crossbar, embraced Yeshua and freed his arms from the upper bonds. Yeshua’s naked, wet body collapsed onto Levi and knocked him to the ground. Levi wanted to heave it onto his shoulders at once, but some thought stopped him. He left on the ground, in the water, the body with its head thrown back and its arms flung wide, and ran, his feet sliding apart in the clay slush, to the other posts. He cut the ropes on them too, and two bodies collapsed onto the ground.
A few minutes passed, and on the top of the hill there remained only these two bodies and three empty posts. The water beat at these bodies and turned them over.
Neither Levi nor Yeshua’s body was on the top of the hill any longer by this time.
